summary: This informational catalog describes 31 available X.500 directory implementations, including servers, clients and interfaces, and revises RFC 1632. It was compiled from submissions by implementors through a web page.

eli5.summary: A shopping catalog listing many kinds of phone books and how they work.

subtitle: A 1997 buyer's guide to 31 X.500 directory servers, clients and gateways, as described by their own makers.

tldr.problem: People who wanted to deploy an X.500 Directory service had no single, easy-to-find source describing which implementations existed and what they could do.
tldr.mechanism: The editors collected descriptions through a WWW form, wrote them up in a common format, and added a keyword index so readers could find implementations by capability, platform or availability.
tldr.outcome: The result is a catalog of 31 implementations (DSAs, DUAs and DUA interfaces) that replaces RFC 1632. It is informational only, and the descriptions were written by implementors, so the editors do not vouch for them.

today: RFC 2116 is Informational and obsoletes RFC 1632. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, but it is a 1997 snapshot, and its entries carry the dates their authors last checked them.

sections.title: Purpose, Scope and Disclaimer
sections.content:
RFC 2116 is an informational catalog of currently available X.500 implementations, both commercial products and openly available ones. It is a revision of RFC 1632, which itself revised RFC 1292. The stated purpose is to give an easily accessible source of information to anyone considering X.500 technology for a Directory service, at a time when Internet X.500 piloting was growing steadily.

The scope is deliberately narrow. The document describes what exists so readers can make informed choices. It does not tell you how to install, run or manage any of these products.

The disclaimer matters. The descriptions were written by implementors and vendors, not by the editors. The editors worked with the authors on uniformity and readability but say they cannot guarantee accuracy, completeness or the stability of the implementations. The memo also states that it does not specify an Internet standard of any kind.
sections.eli5: The catalog is a list of what you can buy or download, not a how-to book. The sellers wrote their own pages, so the people who made the catalog cannot promise every claim is right.

sections.title: How the Catalog Was Compiled
sections.content:
The IDS (Integrated Directory Services) Working Group published the address of a set of on-line description forms on the WWW, hosted as a home page on an InterNIC server. That address was advertised on several directory-related mailing lists. The editors also contacted each contributor to RFC 1632 and asked for an update, so existing entries were refreshed and new ones could be added.

Readers were invited to send comments on both the forms and the content. The IDS Working Group says it will produce new versions when a significant number of substantive comments arrive, or when X.500-related standards documents change significantly. The editors thank the description authors and the IDS Working Group, and especially the editors of RFC 1632, who contributed the nroff source file used to structure their version.
sections.eli5: The editors put a sign-up form on the web and told mailing lists about it. Sellers filled in their pages, and the old catalog's makers shared their layout so the new one could be built on it.

sections.title: DSA, DUA and DUA Interface
sections.content:
The catalog sorts every product into one of three classes.

  • A DSA (Directory System Agent) is an OSI application process that provides the Directory functionality.
  • A DUA (Directory User Agent) is an OSI application process that represents a user in accessing the Directory. It uses the DAP to talk to a DSA.
  • A DUA Interface also represents a user, but it supports only a subset of DAP or uses a protocol different from DAP to talk to a DSA or DUA.

The abstract counts 31 implementations across these three classes. The keyword list also lets an implementation be marked DSA Only, DUA Only, DSA/DUA (both included) or API (it ships with libraries and include files), and LDAP marks a DUA interface program that uses the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol.
sections.eli5: Think of a library. The DSA is the library that holds the books, and the DUA is the helper who walks in and asks for one on your behalf. A DUA interface is a simpler helper who speaks a different, easier language.

sections.title: The Keyword Index
sections.content:
Section 2 defines keywords, which are abbreviated attributes of the implementations. They come from the descriptions themselves. An implementation is indexed under a keyword only when its description explicitly mentions the capability, not by inference, or when its author asked for it.

The keywords are grouped by functional category: availability (for example Free, Commercially Available, Available via FTP, Limited Availability), conformance with international standards (such as DAP, DSP, DISP, DOP, BAC and SAC), conformance with proposed Internet standards, other profiles and schemas, implementation type, internetworking environment, pilot connectivity, miscellaneous features and operating environment.

Table 2-1 lists every implementation with an abbreviation and the page where its description starts. The index that follows lists, under each keyword in alphabetical order, the implementations it applies to, so a reader can look up a platform or a feature and see the matching products.
sections.eli5: The index is like the back of a cookbook: look up an ingredient and it tells you every recipe that uses it. Here the ingredients are things like which computers a product runs on.

sections.title: Internet Standards and RFC Conformance
sections.content:
Several keywords record conformance with RFCs. Those for proposed Internet standards include RFC 1274 (the COSINE and Internet X.500 schema), RFC 1276 (replication and distributed operations extensions), RFC 1277 (encoding network addresses for non-OSI lower layers), RFC 1567 (Directory Monitoring MIB), RFC 1777 (LDAP), RFC 1778, RFC 1779 and RFC 1798 (connection-less LDAP). The memo says that implementations conforming to these proposals have a higher probability of interoperating with others deployed on the Internet.

A second group covers informational and experimental RFCs. The memo says compliance with these is not necessary for interoperability but may enhance functionality. Examples include RFC 1249 (DIXIE), RFC 1558 (LDAP search filter strings), RFC 1617 (naming and structuring guidelines for pilots) and RFC 1803 (recommendations for a production directory service).

A RFC-1006 keyword marks products that run over RFC 1006 on TCP/IP, which the catalog notes is an Internet Standard. Other keywords cover X.25, OSI transport and CLNS.
sections.eli5: Some products follow the Internet's rulebooks, and the catalog tags them. Following them makes it more likely that a product can chat with other products on the Internet.

sections.title: The Implementation Descriptions
sections.content:
Section 3 holds the descriptions, in alphabetical order. Where two products share a name, the responsible organization appears in square brackets. Every description follows one template: name, abstract, compliance with X.500-1988 and with X.500-1993, conformance with proposed Internet standards, consistence with informational and experimental RFCs, interoperability, pilot connectivity, bugs, caveats and limitations, internetworking environment, hardware platforms, software platforms, number of implementations in the field, availability, date last updated, and additional comments.

The pilot connectivity field uses four levels: Not Tested, None, DUA Connectivity and DSA Connectivity. Fields a contributor left empty are marked as not provided by the editor. For example, the A-Window-To-Directory entry, a PC DUA interface designed for use with the Bull X500-DUA product, lists no pilot information.

The entries vary widely. The University of Michigan LDAP package contains a stand-alone LDAP server (slapd), a replication server (slurpd), an LDAP-to-X.500 gateway (ldapd) and client libraries, and its entry says it is used by almost all Internet X.500 sites, with the number of installations unknown. The ISODE Consortium entry describes a source release of an X.500(1993) DSA, and Bull's X500-DS and X500-DUA are described as part of the large Bull OSI offer. Critical Angle X.500 Enabler lets an LDAP-only directory server join X.500 environments by converting DAP and DSP requests into LDAP requests.
sections.eli5: Every seller had to fill in the same form, so you can compare pages side by side. If a seller left a box blank, the editors wrote that no information was provided.

sections.title: Security and What It Leaves Out
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section is one sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo. The individual descriptions do mention security features such as X.509 certification support, simple authentication and access control, but the RFC itself makes no security analysis.

Treat each entry as a snapshot. Each carries a last updated or checked date supplied by its author, and entries cited in this catalog range from products already on sale to products not yet released. The Critical Angle entry, for example, speaks of an initial release scheduled for 4Q96 and a public beta in September 1996.
sections.eli5: The catalog does not say how safe any product is. Each page is only a picture of what the seller said on one particular day.
